solutionCodeJson.name: provision-key.sh
solutionCodeJson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cap phat mot khoa quyen-toi-thieu, ROI TU TAN CONG chinh no.
# Chi chay phep thu THUAN thi ban biet khoa CHAY DUOC.
# Phai chay ca phep thu NGHICH moi biet khoa CHI chay duoc dung viec do.
set -uo pipefail

HOST=${1:?usage: provision-key.sh HOST NAME [VERB]}
NAME=${2:?usage: provision-key.sh HOST NAME [VERB]}
VERB=${3:-status}   # mot dong tu ma lenh bi ep CHAP NHAN (xem bai truoc)
PRIV="./$NAME"
FORCED="/usr/local/bin/$NAME-only.sh"

# ── 1) Khoa ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [ ! -e "$PRIV" ]; then
  ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "$NAME" -f "$PRIV" -N '' -q
fi
KEYLINE=$(cat "$PRIV.pub")
B64=$(awk '{print $2}' "$PRIV.pub")

# ── 2) Cai dat ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# restrict PHAI co. Chi command= thoi thi cai khoa VAN mo duong ham duoc,
# tuc la di vong qua chinh cai vo boc vua dung len.
# LUU Y CU PHAP: than heredoc bat dau ngay o DONG KE TIEP, nen khong duoc
# viet `|| { ... }` o cuoi dong nay — dau ngoac dong se bi nuot vao than
# heredoc va bash bao "unexpected end of file" o tan cuoi file.
# Dat phep kiem SAU dau ket thuc heredoc.
if ssh "$HOST" "OPTS='restrict,command=\"$FORCED\"' LINE='$KEYLINE' B64='$B64' bash -s" <<'REMOTE' >/dev/null
  set -euo pipefail
  mkdir -p ~/.ssh; chmod 700 ~/.ssh; touch ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  grep -qF -- "$B64" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys || \
    printf '%s %s\n' "$OPTS" "$LINE" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
REMOTE
then
  :
else
  echo "khong cai duoc khoa" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Ham goi chung: MOI phep thu deu di qua day, nen khong the co chuyen
# phep thu nay dung tham so khac phep thu kia.
try() { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 -i "$PRIV" "$@"; }

# ── 3) Ket noi co ban PHAI chay truoc ───────────────────────────────
# Neu bo qua buoc nay, mot su co mang se lam ca bon phep thu nghich
# "dat" — ban se bao cao mot cai khoa an toan ma chua he thu gi.
#
# Diem tinh te: KHONG duoc lay "ma thoat khac 0" lam dau hieu that bai o
# day. Mot cai vo boc tot se TU CHOI yeu cau rong (thoat 77), va do la
# no dang lam DUNG viec cua no. Chi rieng 255 moi co nghia "chua bao gio
# ket noi duoc" — dung phan biet cua Module 1.
try "$HOST" "$VERB" </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1
rc=$?
if [ "$rc" -eq 255 ]; then
  echo "ABORT khong ket noi duoc bang khoa moi — chua kiem duoc gi" >&2
  exit 1
fi

leak=0
mark() { if [ "$2" = ok ]; then echo "$1 ok"; else echo "$1 LEAK"; leak=1; fi; }

# ── 4a) Phep thu THUAN ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Lenh bi ep phai chay va in ra thu gi do cho mot dong tu duoc phep.
out=$(try "$HOST" "$VERB" </dev/null 2>/dev/null)
case "$out" in
  ?*) echo "POSITIVE ok" ;;
  *)  echo "POSITIVE failed"; leak=1 ;;
esac

# ── 4b) NGHICH: xin mot shell tuong tac ─────────────────────────────
# Dau hieu quan sat duoc la dong "PTY allocation request failed".
shell_out=$(try -tt "$HOST" </dev/null 2>&1)
case "$shell_out" in
  *"PTY allocation request failed"*) mark "NEG shell" ok ;;
  *) mark "NEG shell" leak ;;
esac

# ── 4c) NGHICH: xin chay lenh khac ──────────────────────────────────
# KHONG duoc xet ma thoat: lenh bi ep tra ve 0 du client xin gi di nua.
# Phai xet NOI DUNG: neu thay "uid=" tuc la `id` da that su chay.
arb_out=$(try "$HOST" id </dev/null 2>/dev/null)
case "$arb_out" in
  *uid=*) mark "NEG arbitrary" leak ;;
  *)      mark "NEG arbitrary" ok ;;
esac

# ── 4d) NGHICH: mo duong ham ────────────────────────────────────────
# CAI BAY LON NHAT CUA CA BAI: voi -L, ssh bind cong o MAY MINH NGAY LAP
# TUC, truoc va doc lap voi viec may chu co dong y hay khong. Nen:
#   - `nc -z 127.0.0.1 15432` LUON thanh cong, ke ca khi duong ham chet;
#   - `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` cung khong cuu duoc, vi voi -L su tu choi
#     chi xay ra luc CO LUU LUONG di qua, chu khong luc thiet lap.
# Log may chu luc do ghi "refused local port forward" — nhung phia client
# thi moi thu trong nhu da mo. Phep thu duy nhat dung la GUI THU GI DO
# qua ong roi xem co byte nao tro ve khong.
tunnel_leak=0
if try -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -L 15432:127.0.0.1:22 -N -f "$HOST" </dev/null 2>/dev/null; then
  sleep 1
  banner=""
  if { exec 9<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/15432; } 2>/dev/null; then
    IFS= read -r -t 3 banner <&9 || banner=""
    exec 9<&-; exec 9>&-
  fi
  pkill -f "15432:127.0.0.1:22" 2>/dev/null || true
  # Co byte SSH tro ve => duong ham that su thong => rang buoc da thung.
  case "$banner" in SSH-*) tunnel_leak=1 ;; esac
fi
if [ "$tunnel_leak" -eq 1 ]; then mark "NEG tunnel" leak; else mark "NEG tunnel" ok; fi

# ── 4e) NGHICH: chuyen tiep agent ───────────────────────────────────
# Doc thang LOI KHAI CUA MAY CHU. Voi -v, client in lai nguyen van dong
# may chu gui sang, liet ke cac tuy chon dang co hieu luc cho khoa nay:
#
#   Co restrict:    Remote: ...authorized_keys:1: key options: command
#   Khong restrict: Remote: ...authorized_keys:1: key options: agent-forwarding
#                   command port-forwarding pty user-rc x11-forwarding
#
# Cach nay tot hon hai cach gian tiep thuong thay: do SSH_AUTH_SOCK o may
# xa thi bi chinh lenh bi ep che mat (no bo qua lenh ban gui), con doan
# theo ma thoat thi khong phan biet duoc "bi tu choi" voi "chay xong".
# Day la may chu tu noi ra, va no bao luon ca pty lan port-forwarding.
optline=$(try -v -A "$HOST" "$VERB" </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -m1 'key options:')
case "$optline" in
  *agent-forwarding*) mark "NEG agent" leak ;;
  *)                  mark "NEG agent" ok ;;
esac

# ── 5) Ket luan ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if [ "$leak" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "RESULT locked"
  exit 0
fi
echo "RESULT leaking"
exit 6

exercises.solutionExplanationHtml:
Negative tests are the deliverable. The positive test confirms the key works, which is what a provisioning script normally checks and is exactly the thing that would still be true if the restrictions were silently absent. Writing command="…" without restrict — a plausible typo, and the configuration many tutorials show — produces a key whose forced command runs perfectly and which can still open -L 5432:localhost:5432 straight to Postgres, bypassing the wrapper it was built around. Only an attempt to do the forbidden thing surfaces that.

Three of the four negative tests need a specific technique, because the naive version scores a leak as a pass.

  • Arbitrary command: exit status is useless. A forced command returns its own status regardless of what the client requested, so try "$HOST" id exits 0 whether id ran or not. The test has to inspect the output and look for uid=, which appears only if id genuinely executed.
  • Tunnel: this one is the trap that catches almost everyone, and it fails in the safe-looking direction. With -L, ssh binds the local port on your own machine immediately, independently of whether the server agrees to the forward. So nc -z 127.0.0.1 15432 reports success, and a test built on that reports LEAK for a properly restricted key. ExitOnForwardFailure=yes does not rescue it either: for a local forward the refusal happens when traffic arrives, not at setup, so ssh still exits 0. Meanwhile the server log says exactly what happened — refused local port forward: originator 127.0.0.1 port 64772, target localhost port 22. The only honest client-side test is to push bytes through the forward and see whether anything comes back.
  • Agent: asking whether -A "worked" has no direct answer, so the test observes the consequence — whether SSH_AUTH_SOCK is set to a real path in the remote environment. A restricted key leaves it empty.

The connectivity pre-check prevents the worst possible outcome for a security tool: a false all-clear. If the host is unreachable, every negative test fails to connect, every failure looks like a refusal, and the script prints four ok lines and RESULT locked for a key it never tested. Establishing that a basic connection succeeds first means each subsequent failure can be attributed to the restriction rather than to the network. This is the same principle as Module 1's connection doctor and as this track's recurring rule — verify the checker before you trust what it reports.

Routing every connection through one try() helper is what keeps the tests comparable. Five hand-written ssh invocations drift apart, and once the positive test and the negative tests are not using the same identity settings, the comparison between them stops meaning anything.
